prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, in which magic-wavelength trapping allows many atoms to be interrogated free of Doppler, recoil and trap-induced shifts, bringing optical frequency standards to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I keep the optical lattice clock as my preferred single-part prize with Katori and Ye, and the exchange has strengthened rather than weakened my reasons. The chair asks what is new relative to 2005 and 2012. My answer is that the 2005 prize rewarded the frequency comb and laser stabilisation, which are the ruler, and the 2012 prize rewarded control of a single quantum system, an ion, which is accurate but statistically limited by one particle. Katori's magic-wavelength idea is a different physical step: it makes the trapping potential itself invisible to the clock transition, so that thousands of atoms are confined Doppler- and recoil-free and interrogated in parallel. That converts the clock into a controlled many-body quantum system, and Ye's group showed what this buys: 10^-18 systematic uncertainty, instability that averages down in hours instead of weeks, millimetre-scale gravitational redshift across a sample, and interactions and spin physics in the lattice that had to be understood in every physical detail. This is a result I can judge with the tests I trust, namely whether it opened a new regime and whether independent laboratories reproduce it. JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, SYRTE, PTB and NIST build different clocks and they agree. The citation should name the magic-wavelength lattice as the discovery, not the number and not the future redefinition of the second, which I do not think should be in the citation or decide the timing. After round 1 the picture is also clear: B040 and B016 each have an unresolved credit problem that the supplied text cannot settle, while the two-name credit for B045 is agreed by all five members who proposed it.
statement.case_against: The distinctness argument is real and I do not dismiss it: a sceptic can say the lattice clock is the natural next layer on comb and ion-clock technology, with its largest consequences, the redefinition of the second, geodesy and dark-matter searches, still prospective. A two-name credit also leaves out Lemonde and the SYRTE group, Takamoto in Katori's group, and Hall-type laser stabilisation, and the priority of Katori's proposal against early strontium lattice work should be checked before a final vote. In addition, I still regard circuit QED as the scientifically stronger case for opening a new regime of light-matter interaction, so my preference for B045 is partly a judgement about timing, maturity and the absence of an overlapping recent prize. I accept that this judgement could be wrong if the committee reads the lattice clock as a refinement.

responses.point: Kroll argues that the lattice clock is distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes because it addresses Doppler, recoil and quantum-projection-noise limits in a different way, and that B045 is the better choice this year than B026 because it has no overlap with the 2025 prize and my own flagged conflict would complicate B026.
responses.response: I agree, and I would sharpen it into the committee's answer to the chair's question: comb equals the ruler (2005), ion control equals one particle (2012), magic-wavelength lattice equals many atoms in a controlled environment, which is a different physical lever on the same measurement problem. On B026, I accept your argument and have moved my fallbacks away from it. I cannot take part in deciding it, and I no longer want my fallback ranking to carry a ballot I should not weigh. I also note your Hall-laboratory connection; I do not think it touches Katori or Ye and I would regard it as minor, but it should stay on the record.

responses.point: Lindroth supports B045 as the one candidate with a clean two-person credit, but lists priority questions (early Sr lattice work, Lemonde and SYRTE, Takamoto, Hall's stabilisation) and asks whether waiting for the redefinition of the second would strengthen or only delay the case.
responses.response: On waiting, I think it would only delay. The physics case does not depend on the redefinition, which is a metrological and political decision and may take until the end of the decade, and the lattice clocks are already being used in comparisons, relativistic geodesy and constants tests. The citation should therefore rest on the magic-wavelength lattice and the 10^-18 demonstrations. On priority, I would want a note in the committee's working papers that Takamoto and the SYRTE group demonstrated early Sr lattice clocks and that we credit Katori for the concept; I would not enlarge to a third name, because the cleanest two-person credit on the table is the main thing B045 has going for it. We agree on B007 as a serious fallback.

responses.point: Pearce, who prefers B016 and Halzen-Karle, concedes that the attribution cannot be settled from the supplied text and that B045 is probably the consensus candidate, while urging that the citation cover only the diffuse flux.
responses.response: I think that candour is what the committee needs. I judge the diffuse flux to be established by several independent analysis channels and I would not oppose B016 if the credit between Halzen, Karle, AMANDA and other IceCube leaders can be settled; it is why I now list it as an alternative. But I defer to Pearce and Danielsson on that credit, and until it is resolved I would rather vote for a candidate whose names no one disputes. I am glad that Pearce restricts the citation to the diffuse flux, since that is the part that does not depend on a single experiment.

responses.point: Danielsson says the prize for IceCube would be premature if the source identifications must be confirmed first and that B045 is the safer, broader alternative, but also argues that a quantum-technology prize such as B026 should be delayed after 2025.
responses.response: I agree on the second point and have changed my fallbacks accordingly: I withdraw B026 from my alternatives because of the 2025 prize and my own conflict, and I would hold it for a later year. On the first, your own argument that B045 is the safer alternative is the honest summary of where I am. I do want to challenge one thing, which is the suggestion that the clock is merely an enabling tool. It is an enabling tool in the sense that a spectrometer is, but the discovery rewarded is the identification of the magic wavelength and what it does to the many-atom system, and that is physics.

responses.point: Mehlig, Eriksson and Olsson prefer B040 with Kane, Mele and Molenkamp, arguing that the chain from the Z2 classification to the HgTe edge transport is traceable, fifteen years of confirmation have stabilised it, and recognition is overdue.
responses.response: I defer on the condensed-matter physics and I find the Z2 argument persuasive as science. My difficulty is the credit, and the round-1 files confirm that it is not only my difficulty: the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal that told Molenkamp which material to use lies outside the trio, Zhang is deceased, and Hasan's 3D spectroscopy is omitted by the same trio. Mehlig and Olsson's own question about whether a different split is fairer shows that three names do not reach the whole discovery. I also hear the 2016 argument as real but secondary. If the three of you can agree a split with an explicit answer on Hasan and BHZ, I would take B040 seriously as a fallback, but I do not think that is settled and I cannot supply it from my own field.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts the answer to the chair's question, that the magic-wavelength lattice is a distinct many-atom advance and not a refinement of the 2005 comb or 2012 ion-control prizes.

Whether Katori's priority for the magic-wavelength concept, and the roles of Takamoto, Lemonde and the SYRTE group, are fairly captured by a two-name credit; I cannot verify the dates from the supplied text.

Whether the B040 camp can settle a defensible trio with a clear position on Hasan and the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal, and whether B016 can settle its Halzen-Karle credit; both could change the comparison, and I rely on colleagues for these fields.
Whether delay would strengthen B045 through a redefinition of the second or only postpone a mature prize; I lean towards the latter.
statement.conflict_note: Unchanged in substance. As director of WACQT and a theorist in superconducting circuits at Chalmers, I am close to circuit QED (B026) and to the circuit-based parts of B008, and I will recuse myself from deciding both. For that reason I have removed B026 from my alternatives, although I still rate its physics highly. I also note that Kroll, Mehlig and Olsson have mentioned Chalmers or Gothenburg proximity or WACQT overlap; none of this involves B045, B007, B016 or B040. I have no apparent personal tie to Katori or Ye, and the connection to Hall-type laser stabilisation that Kroll disclosed does not touch my own position.
